rows.question: Why couldn't Apollo 13's command module CO2 canisters be used directly in the lunar module?
rows.answer:
The search results explain the physical mismatch, though not in full engineering detail. The command module's lithium hydroxide canisters were square and the lunar module's were round. Because the shapes didn't fit the lunar module's receptacles, the crew had to improvise. Engineers devised an adapter from hoses, cardboard, plastic bags and tape, and the crew built it from radioed instructions.

The results don't go further into why the lunar module's receptacles required round canisters, so that detail isn't covered here.

rows.question: Why did the Apollo Guidance Computer keep flying through the Apollo 11 alarms?
rows.answer:
The search results don't establish a sourced cause. The Apollo 11 Mission Report says the alarms left the core guidance and control chain working, since they did not degrade any primary guidance or control function. The alarms did affect the crew, interfering with the crew's early assessment of the landing approach.

The only explanation for why the computer kept running is an unsourced note, labeled as derived, that credits the software's scheduling design (the software engineering division at the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory that developed Apollo on-board flight software led by Margaret Hamilton). That note is not backed by a mission record in these results, so I can't confirm it from them.

rows.question: Which company's revised specification set the voltage that the Apollo 13 tank switches could not handle?
rows.answer:
North American Aviation is the company whose revision matters here. Its heater specification for the oxygen tank was changed to 65 volts in 1965. Revised the oxygen tank heater specification in 1965 to run at 65 volts. The switches had been designed for a lower voltage, since its thermostatic switches were built to a 1962 specification for 28 volts DC.

The mismatch came from the switches not being updated after that change. Heater power rose to 65 volts in 1965, yet the switches stayed as they were. Beech Aircraft manufactured the tanks for North American, and it was Beech that did not change the tank thermostatic switches when the heater specification moved to 65 volts. North American's documentation reviews also missed the problem, as they missed that the tank's thermostatic switches were never changed.

rows.question: Which company built the craft that kept the Apollo 13 astronauts alive after their main ship was crippled?
